title: Printing & Finishing
description: Commercial printing processes and surface finishes that protect, enhance and differentiate paper and board products.
content_html:
Why Printing and Finishing Matter

A perfectly constructed carton with no print is worthless at point of sale. Printing communicates brand identity, product information, legal requirements and visual appeal. Finishing — applying a coating, texture or foil over the printed surface — adds protection, elevates perceived quality and can make a product physically stand out on a shelf. Together, printing and finishing are the processes that transform a blank piece of board into the persuasive, durable, eye-catching packaging or graphic product a designer has conceived. Understanding these processes allows a designer to specify them correctly in a manufacturing brief and to appreciate why they cost what they do.

Offset Lithography

Offset lithography is the world’s most widely used commercial printing process for paper and board. It exploits the principle that oil and water repel each other. A printing plate (typically aluminium, around 0.3 mm thick) is chemically treated so that image areas attract oil-based ink and reject water, while non-image areas attract water and reject ink. The inked image is then transferred (‘offset’) from the plate to a rubber blanket cylinder, and from there to the paper or board. The rubber blanket conforms to the surface of the substrate, giving sharper results than direct plate-to-paper printing. Full-colour printing uses four plates in sequence: Cyan, Magenta, Yellow and Key (Black) — the CMYK process. Each colour is printed as a pattern of microscopic halftone dots; the eye blends them to produce the full spectrum of visible colours. Lithography is cost-effective at runs of several thousand sheets upward, producing consistent, high-quality results at high speed.

Screen Printing

Screen printing forces ink through a fine mesh screen onto the substrate. Areas of the screen that should not print are blocked with a photochemically applied stencil; ink is pushed through open mesh areas with a rubber squeegee. Each colour requires a separate screen. Screen printing deposits a thick, opaque layer of ink, producing vivid, high-impact colours that are ideal for printing on dark or textured substrates. Unlike lithography, screen printing works on rigid, three-dimensional objects as well as flat sheets — bottles, tins, clothing and circuit boards can all be screen-printed. It is economical for short runs or for applications requiring specialist inks (fluorescent, metallic, UV-reactive, conductive) that cannot be used in a litho press.

Flexography

Flexography uses a flexible polymer relief plate mounted on a rotating cylinder. Image areas are raised above the non-image surface and pick up ink from an anilox roller (a cylinder engraved with tiny cells that control ink volume). The inked image is then printed directly onto the substrate. Flexographic inks dry very rapidly by evaporation or UV curing, making the process suited to continuous-feed production lines. Flexography is the dominant process for printing on corrugated board, plastic carrier bags, food wrappers and newspaper supplements — any application requiring fast drying on a non-absorbent or structurally delicate substrate. Print quality is slightly lower than lithography, particularly for fine detail and photographic images.

Digital and Inkjet Printing

Digital printing — including large-format inkjet and electrostatic toner-based printing — requires no printing plates. The image is sent directly from a computer file to the print engine, where microscopic droplets of CMYK (and sometimes additional) inks are jetted or fused onto the substrate. The key advantages are zero set-up cost (no plates to make), instant changeover between different designs, and the ability to personalise each sheet differently (variable data printing). These properties make digital printing ideal for short runs, prototypes and personalised packaging. The main limitations are higher cost per unit at large volumes compared with lithography, and restrictions on the range of substrates and inks that can be used. Large-format inkjet printers are standard in school design departments and commercial sign-making workshops.

Key Fact

Full-colour offset lithography uses four ink colours: Cyan, Magenta, Yellow and Key (Black) — abbreviated CMYK. Each colour is printed separately as halftone dots. Where all four overlap at full density, the result is a near-black. The eye blends the dots at normal reading distance to perceive continuous tones and millions of intermediate colours from just four inks.

Varnishing

Varnish is a clear liquid coating applied over a printed surface to protect the ink from abrasion, moisture and fingerprints, and to enhance the visual finish. Gloss varnish reflects light, making colours appear brighter and more saturated. Matt varnish absorbs light, giving a flat, sophisticated appearance with low glare. Satin (or silk) varnish sits between the two extremes. Varnish can be applied over the entire sheet (flood varnish) or selectively over specific design elements using a printing plate (spot varnish). UV spot varnish is applied to a precise area and instantly cured by ultraviolet light, creating a high-gloss, raised tactile effect. A common technique is soft-touch varnish, which creates a velvety, almost rubberised surface texture that feels luxurious and discourages fingerprinting.

Lamination

Lamination bonds a thin transparent film (typically biaxially-oriented polypropylene, BOPP) to the printed surface using heat and pressure or adhesive. Like varnish, it is available in gloss, matt and satin finishes. Lamination offers considerably more protection than varnish — it is waterproof, scuff-resistant and significantly increases the structural stiffness of the board. For this reason, lamination is the standard finish for hardback book covers, premium food packaging, folded leaflets and retail bags. The main environmental drawback is that laminated paper and board is more difficult to recycle, as the plastic film must be separated from the fibre.

Key Fact

UV spot varnish is applied selectively to specific design elements (e.g. a logo or product image) and cured instantly by ultraviolet light. The result is a high-gloss, slightly raised area that contrasts with the surrounding matt or satin finish, drawing the eye and the fingertip to the key visual element. This technique is widely used on premium packaging, luxury brochures and book covers.

Embossing and Debossing

Embossing uses a matched pair of male and female metal dies pressed together with the board between them, raising a design element above the surface in relief. Debossing uses the same principle but presses the image into the surface, creating a sunken impression. Both processes can be done blind (no ink or foil, relying on the shadow and highlight of the relief) or combined with foil blocking. Embossing is used on premium packaging, business cards and stationery to add a tactile quality that immediately communicates high value.

Foil Blocking

Foil blocking (also called hot foil stamping) uses a heated metal die to press a thin metallic foil onto the surface of the board. Under heat and pressure, the foil transfers from its carrier film to the board surface. Gold, silver, holographic and coloured foils are all available. Foil blocking produces a brilliant, mirror-like metallic finish that cannot be achieved by printing with metallic ink alone. It is used on luxury product packaging, book covers, greetings cards and security documents. Foil blocking can be combined with embossing in a single press operation for maximum visual and tactile impact.

Every surface finish serves one or more of three purposes: protection, aesthetics and function. Gloss lamination on a food-service menu protects the print from food and liquid spills (protection), makes colours appear brighter (aesthetics) and allows the surface to be wiped clean (function). UV spot varnish on a luxury perfume carton adds no measurable protection but dramatically improves visual appeal at point of sale (pure aesthetics). Foil blocking on a security document provides a holographic element that is difficult to counterfeit (function). Designers must specify finishes with clear reasons linked to the product’s performance requirements, not just because they ‘look nice’.

Cost also determines finish choice: flood lamination adds approximately 5–15% to the print cost; UV spot varnish is more expensive per unit because it requires an additional print pass; foil blocking costs more again because each colour of foil requires a separate die. At low production volumes, digital spot varnish (applied by an inkjet-based digital press) offers a cheaper alternative to UV spot, though with slightly less tactile relief.

Offset lithography: medium-to-high volume, highest quality for paper and board, four-plate CMYK, slow set-up. Screen printing: short-to-medium run, thick opaque ink, specialist substrates including three-dimensional objects. Flexography: continuous-feed, fast-drying inks, lower quality, corrugated and film substrates. Digital/inkjet: very short run or one-offs, no plates, variable data, moderate quality. A question asking you to justify a printing process choice should always reference: volume of production, substrate type, print quality required and set-up cost.
exam_tip_html: When comparing printing processes in an exam, structure your answer around four criteria: volume (short, medium, long run), substrate (paper, board, film, 3D object), quality (photographic detail, flat colour) and cost (set-up vs unit cost). For finishing questions, always state why a finish is applied — protection, aesthetics or function — and link it to a specific product context. Writing ‘lamination makes it shiny’ misses the point; ‘gloss lamination protects the printed surface from scuffing during transit and increases perceived quality at point of sale’ answers correctly.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four main commercial printing processes are offset lithography (high-volume, CMYK, highest quality), screen printing (short run, thick ink, 3D substrates), flexography (continuous-feed, corrugated and film packaging) and digital inkjet (no plates, short run, variable data).
  • Surface finishes include varnishing (gloss, matt, UV spot), lamination (waterproof film bonded over print), embossing and debossing (tactile relief via metal dies) and foil blocking (metallic transfer under heat and pressure).
  • Every finish serves a defined purpose: protection (lamination on a menu), aesthetics (UV spot on a perfume carton) or function (holographic foil on a security document). Designers must justify finish choices against the product brief, not just visual preference.

glossary_terms.definition: A printing process in which ink is transferred from a flat, chemically treated plate to a rubber blanket roller, and then offset onto the substrate; the dominant commercial process for medium to high volume print runs.
A rotary printing process using flexible polymer relief plates and fast-drying inks; widely used for printing directly onto corrugated board, plastic films and food packaging.
A finishing process using metal dies to press a design into the surface of paper or board, raising (emboss) or sinking (deboss) the image for a tactile, three-dimensional effect.
A selectively applied clear varnish cured instantly by ultraviolet light, creating a high-gloss, slightly raised tactile finish over specific design elements.

practice_questions.text:
Which printing process uses flexible polymer relief plates and is the dominant method for printing onto corrugated board?
A) Offset lithography
B) Screen printing
C) Flexography
D) Digital inkjet
Name the four ink colours used in full-colour offset lithographic printing.
practice_questions.marks: All four required for 2 marks: Cyan, Magenta, Yellow, Key (Black). Accept CMYK as the abbreviation if the full names or colours are given alongside. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how UV spot varnish is applied to a printed board surface and explain its effect.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per clear, distinct point up to 3:
- UV spot varnish is applied selectively over specific design elements (e.g. a logo or image) using a printing plate or digital print engine.
- The varnish is cured instantly by exposure to ultraviolet light, hardening to a high-gloss, slightly raised surface.
- The contrast between the glossy spot-varnished area and the surrounding matt or satin surface draws the eye and adds a tactile quality that communicates premium value. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a packaging designer would specify digital inkjet printing rather than offset lithography for a run of 200 personalised gift boxes.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Digital inkjet requires no printing plates, so there is no plate-making set-up cost regardless of how many designs are printed.
- Each box can carry a different name or image (variable data printing) without any additional cost or changeover time, which is essential for personalised gifting.
- At 200 units, the set-up cost of making four lithographic plates would make the per-unit cost very high, far exceeding the cost of digital printing.
- Lithography is only economical at volumes of several thousand sheets, where the fixed plate cost is spread over a large number of units. [4 marks: 1 mark per clear, developed point]

practice_questions.text: Explain the differences between gloss lamination and UV spot varnish as surface finishing techniques, including why each is applied and the effect each produces on a printed carton.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
- Gloss lamination bonds a transparent BOPP film across the entire printed surface (flood application), making it waterproof, scuff-resistant and increasing board stiffness.
- UV spot varnish is applied selectively to specific areas of the printed design, creating a high-gloss, slightly raised tactile contrast against the surrounding surface.
- Lamination is primarily functional: it protects the surface from moisture, abrasion and handling, making it suitable for products that experience heavy use (menus, carrier bags, brochure covers).
- UV spot varnish is primarily aesthetic: it creates a premium visual and tactile quality by highlighting key design elements such as logos or product images.
- Lamination adds more measurable protection but makes the board harder to recycle; UV spot varnish adds less protection but is thinner and less of a recycling barrier.
[6 marks - Mastering: Both processes fully described and contrasted in terms of application method, purpose and carton context. Secure: Both described with some contrast; purpose linked but not fully developed. Developing: One process well described; second superficial. Emerging: Vague reference to one process only.]

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of using offset lithography compared with screen printing for producing 50,000 units of printed retail packaging.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of offset lithography:
- Produces the highest quality photographic image reproduction via CMYK halftone dot printing, suitable for detailed product photography on packaging.
- At 50,000 units, the fixed cost of making four printing plates is easily amortised across the run, giving a very low cost per sheet.
- High-speed rotary presses can print thousands of sheets per hour, meeting a tight production schedule.
- Consistent, repeatable colour across the entire run is maintained by ink density controls, important for brand colour accuracy.
Disadvantages of offset lithography:
- Four plates must be made for a full-colour job, adding a significant set-up cost that makes it uneconomical for short runs.
- Lithography works best on flat sheets of paper and board; it cannot easily print onto corrugated or three-dimensional substrates.
- Any design change (e.g. a regulatory update on food packaging) requires a new plate, adding cost and delay.
Advantages of screen printing at 50,000 units:
- Screen printing deposits a thick, opaque ink layer that can print on dark or textured boards where lithography would produce dull, washed-out colours.
- Specialist inks (metallic, UV-reactive, tactile) can be used in screen printing that are not compatible with lithographic presses.
Disadvantages:
- Screen printing is significantly slower than lithography and more expensive per unit at high volumes, making 50,000 units costly.
- Each colour requires a separate screen set-up, and fine photographic detail is harder to achieve than with lithographic halftone dots.
[8 marks - Mastering: Sustained, balanced comparison with at least two developed points for each process, linked to the 50,000-unit context. Secure: Two points per process with some development. Developing: Points listed with limited development; little balance. Emerging: One-sided or very superficial response.]

knowledge_checks.q: Which printing process requires no printing plates and allows a different design to be printed on every sheet?
What does CMYK stand for in full-colour printing?
Foil blocking uses a heated metal die to transfer a metallic foil onto board under _____ and pressure.
Embossing raises a design in relief using a matched pair of _____ dies.
Match each finishing technique to its primary purpose:
right: Waterproof, scuff-resistant protection across the whole surface
Selective high-gloss tactile highlight on a logo or image
Brilliant metallic finish transferred by heat and pressure

flashcard_questions.q: What principle does offset lithography exploit to keep ink on image areas only?
flashcard_questions.a: Oil-based ink and water repel each other; image areas attract ink, non-image areas attract water.

flashcard_questions.q: What does CMYK stand for in commercial printing?
flashcard_questions.a: It refers to the four process inks — cyan, magenta, yellow and key black — layered to reproduce full-colour images in commercial printing.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is flexography suited to printing on corrugated board?
flashcard_questions.a: Its flexible polymer plates and fast-drying inks print directly onto uneven surfaces without crushing the flutes.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main advantage of digital inkjet printing for packaging?
flashcard_questions.a: No plates are needed, so each sheet can carry a different design (variable data) with zero set-up cost.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between gloss and matt varnish?
flashcard_questions.a: Gloss reflects light to make colours appear brighter; matt absorbs light for a flat, sophisticated appearance.
A selectively applied clear varnish cured instantly by UV light, creating a high-gloss, raised tactile highlight.

flashcard_questions.q: How does lamination differ from varnishing in terms of protection?
flashcard_questions.a: Lamination bonds a plastic film to the surface, making it waterproof and scuff-resistant; varnish offers less protection.
Using matched metal dies to press a design so it is raised above the surrounding surface in relief.

flashcard_questions.q: What is foil blocking and what finish does it produce?
flashcard_questions.a: A heated metal die transfers metallic foil under pressure, producing a brilliant mirror-like metallic surface.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is screen printing preferred for printing on dark or textured substrates?
flashcard_questions.a: It deposits a thick, opaque ink layer that shows clearly on dark or uneven surfaces.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one environmental drawback of gloss lamination on paper packaging.
flashcard_questions.a: The plastic film is difficult to separate from the paper fibre, making laminated board harder to recycle.

flashcard_questions.q: What does an anilox roller do in a flexographic printing press?
flashcard_questions.a: It is a cylinder with tiny engraved cells that deliver a controlled, consistent volume of ink to the printing plate.
